items.article_text_original: MHRA sets out regulatory approach to next generation innovation A round-up of the agency's announcements during London Life Sciences Week 2026, including at the inaugural DIA-MHRA Global Summit. London Life Sciences Week is a collaborative effort, connecting over 5000 attendees at over 100 events across the capital. It is co-produced by London & Partners and the BioIndustry Association and supported by the Office for Life Sciences, Office for Investment and the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency. Jefferies is the platinum sponsor. During London Life Sciences Week 2026, the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) has announced a package of new initiatives. These are designed to give innovators earlier support, anticipate the scientific and regulatory challenges of emerging technologies, and strengthen the UK’s environment for developing new medicines and healthcare products. Many of the announcements were made at the inaugural DIA-MHRA Global Summit, held in London on 16 and 17 November. The MHRA and the Drug Information Association (DIA) hosted the summit jointly. It brought together international regulators, industry leaders, researchers, healthcare professionals and patient representatives to explore how global collaboration can support innovation and help it reach patients faster. Across women’s health, clinical research, AI, manufacturing, advanced therapeutics and rare disease, the week showed how better regulation means better evidence, clearer routes for innovators and greater potential for patient benefit. MHRA Chief Executive Lawrence Tallon said: “Science and technology are moving quickly, and regulation needs to anticipate what is coming rather than simply respond to it. Across London Life Sciences Week, we have shown how the MHRA is changing the way we work: engaging earlier with innovators, giving greater regulatory clarity and working with trusted international partners to tackle shared challenges. Our aim is simple: to maintain high standards of safety while creating the conditions in which promising new medicines and technologies can be developed, tested and reach patients sooner. That is good for patients, good for innovation and good for the UK’s position as a global life sciences leader.” Closing evidence gaps in women’s health On 16 November, the MHRA launched a new Women’s Health Programme. It aims to support innovation in women’s health and to improve understanding of how the risks and benefits of medicines and medical devices may differ for women. Women make up 51% of the population but have historically been underrepresented in clinical research. An MHRA analysis of all 4,616 UK clinical trial applications submitted between 2019 and 2023 found that pregnant women were represented in just 1.1% of trials, and breastfeeding women in 0.6%. The programme will bring together patients, researchers, healthcare professionals and industry to strengthen the available evidence, while maintaining the MHRA’s standards of safety, quality and effectiveness. It was shaped by patients, including through the MHRA’s Patient and Public Community and a focus group delivered by the Patients Association. Read more: MHRA launches new programme to tackle evidence gaps on women’s health The UK-Singapore Regulatory Innovation Corridor goes live The UK-Singapore Regulatory Innovation Corridor has entered its first live phase. The MHRA and Singapore’s Health Sciences Authority (HSA) are working together with Apriori Bio, a Flagship Pioneering company, on an AI-enabled approach to selecting influenza vaccine antigens. The aim is to better predict how influenza viruses will evolve and to inform vaccines that offer broader and longer-lasting protection. Earlier, coordinated engagement between two trusted regulators can help address scientific and regulatory questions about emerging technologies sooner. Each authority keeps its own responsibilities and standards. Experience from this initial phase will inform its future development, with a view to broaden participation from 2027. Modernising the regulation of gene therapies On 19 November, the government published its response to the consultation on the regulation of gene therapy medicinal products. The consultation was led jointly by the MHRA and the Department of Health in Northern Ireland. The response confirms plans to modernise the legal definition of gene therapy medicinal products so that certain synthetic gene therapies and novel genome-editing treatments can be regulated under the UK’s established advanced therapies framework. The proposals were supported by 83% of respondents. The changes will give developers greater certainty about how their medicines are classified and what regulatory requirements apply. The existing approval process and the standards for safety, quality and efficacy will not change, and medicines that are already licensed will not need to be reclassified. The changes are subject to international notification procedures and parliamentary approval. They will amend the Human Medicines Regulations 2012. MHRA Executive Director Operations, Julian Beach, said: “Scientific advances are opening up new possibilities for innovative gene therapies, and it is important that regulation keeps pace. By providing greater certainty for developers, we can help attract investment, strengthen the UK’s position as a leader in life sciences and support the development of potentially life-saving new treatments for patients.” Read more: Government backs modernisation of gene therapy definitions - GOV.UK AdvanceGxP: earlier support for advanced manufacturing On 18 November, Science, Innovation and Investment Minister Chris McDonald MP announced a new MHRA service, AdvanceGxP, in his closing speech at the summit. AdvanceGxP will give developers earlier practical support on how Good Practice standards apply to new manufacturing technologies. These include personalised treatments made at or near hospitals and clinics, manufacturing in space, and the use of AI, robotics and automation. The MHRA has secured funding from the Office for Life Sciences to recruit a specialist team and develop and test the service, which will initially focus on advanced manufacturing. The MHRA’s Chief Executive, Lawrence Tallon, said: “We want the UK to be a place where the next generation of innovative medicines can be developed and made. Giving developers practical support earlier can help solve problems before they cause delays, build confidence to invest and make it easier for promising new approaches to grow and scale here.” Read more: New MHRA service to support medicines innovation and strengthen UK manufacturing - GOV.UK A significant step forward for international regulatory collaboration : ACCESS The Access Consortium, which brings together the regulators of Australia, Canada, Singapore, Switzerland and the UK, has agreed to use a new Trusted Regulatory Space. This is a secure platform that will allow closer and more efficient work-sharing between the five authorities. At their meeting in London during the week, the Access Heads of Agencies also endorsed plans to strengthen work-sharing procedures for new active substances, building on growing collaboration and industry engagement in 2026. Work-sharing helps regulators to reduce duplication and address common challenges together. Each authority keeps its own responsibilities and standards and makes its own decisions on whether to authorise a medicine in its own country. The MHRA holds the Access Chair for 2026 and will hand it to Australia’s Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) in 2027. MHRA Chief Executive and Access Chair for 2026, Lawrence Tallon, said: “Access is moving from ambition into practical delivery. By reducing unnecessary duplication and increasing regulatory cooperation, we support faster access to safe and effective medicines for patients, as set out in our Growth Manifesto.”] Professor Tony Lawler, Head of the TGA and incoming Access Chair for 2027, said: “International collaboration between regulators is increasingly important as we respond to a rapidly evolving global medicines environment. I look forward to building on this strong foundation and continuing to strengthen practical cooperation across our five agencies.” International cooperation: Saudi Arabia The MHRA and the Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to strengthen their regulatory partnership. The MoU was signed at the DIA-MHRA Global Summit by MHRA Chief Executive Lawrence Tallon and His Excellency Prof Hisham Saad Aldjadhey, Chief Executive Officer of the SFDA. The MoU provides a framework for closer cooperation, including exchanging regulatory and scientific information and expertise, and technical capacity building. It covers medicines, biologics, medical devices, advanced therapies and other products within the two regulators’ remits. The two organisations have also identified an initial programme of work. This includes rare diseases, AI-enabled medical devices, pharmacopoeia and regulatory standards, and regulatory science. On rare diseases, the MHRA and SFDA intend to explore a joint white paper, which will consider how the UK’s and Saudi Arabia’s complementary strengths in areas including genomics, clinical research and healthcare data could support the development of therapies for conditions affecting small and dispersed patient populations. Working together helps regulators learn from one another, keep pace with fast-moving science and technology, and find ways to make regulation more efficient while maintaining robust standards. The MoU is a framework for cooperation and is not legally binding. Each authority keeps its own responsibilities and standards. What this means for innovators The MHRA is creating opportunities for earlier engagement and clearer regulatory support as new technologies emerge. Innovators developing eligible technologies can follow the progress of the programmes above and explore the relevant routes as they become available. By combining scientific expertise with international collaboration, the MHRA is working to anticipate what is coming and to help promising innovation translate into benefits for patients.

items.article_text_original: Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, 23 November 2026 – African Heads of State and Government gathered to open the Fifth International Conference on Public Health in Africa (CPHIA 2026), calling for greater domestic investment, national ownership and accountability to advance the continent’s health security and sovereignty. Co-hosted by the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) and the Government of Ethiopia, the conference opened at the Addis International Convention Centre (AICC). Highlights included the launch of the African Union Champions’ Roadmap on reproductive, maternal and child health, the presentation of the Artificial Intelligence and Digital Health Championship, and recognition of outstanding contributions to public health. The opening brought together H.E. Abiy Ahmed Ali (PhD), the Prime Minister of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia; H.E. Évariste Ndayishimiye, the President of the Republic of Burundi and Chairperson of the African Union; H.E. Samia Suluhu Hassan, the President of the United Republic of Tanzania; H.E. Dr Julius Maada Bio, the President of the Republic of Sierra Leone; H.E. Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, the Chairperson of the African Union Commission; and H.E. Dr Jean Kaseya, the Africa CDC Director General, alongside ministers, senior government representatives, public health leaders and partners. Running from 23 to 27 November under the theme “Africa’s Health Security and Sovereignty: Transformation from Health Dependency and Vulnerability to Ownership and Resilience,” the conference comes amid declining external health financing and persistent public health threats, underscoring the need for stronger national institutions and sustainable health financing. Africa CDC calls for greater African ownership In his welcome address, Dr. Jean Kaseya emphasised the responsibilities that accompany health sovereignty, including good governance and accountability. “CPHIA is not a conference. CPHIA is a movement, a movement for Africa’s security and sovereignty. We in Africa understood that sovereignty is coming with responsibility. Responsibility is coming with good governance, trust and accountability,” he said. This year’s conference coincides with a decade of Africa CDC’s work in advancing continental public health cooperation, supporting Member States in disease surveillance, emergency preparedness and response, workforce development and regional coordination. Advancing maternal and child health The opening featured the launch of the African Union Champions’ Continental Roadmap on Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health (RMNCAH) 2026–2030, championed by President Hassan.The roadmap seeks to accelerate progress towards three objectives, known as the Three Zeros: zero home deliveries, zero preventable maternal and newborn deaths, and zero unvaccinated children. “The success of this roadmap will depend on effective national implementation, and I therefore call upon all African Union Member States to designate empowered national focal points and integrate the Three Zeros into their existing national health strategies,” President Hassan said. She called for expanded access to skilled, respectful maternity care and routine childhood vaccination, particularly in underserved communities. Drawing on Tanzania’s experience in strengthening health infrastructure and services, she announced an initial commitment of 60 scholarships for specialised training in midwifery, anaesthesia, obstetrics and gynaecology and neonatal care, alongside shorter competency-based training opportunities. Artificial intelligence and digital health Ethiopia, under H.E Prime Minister Dr Abiy Ahmed, presented its African Union Artificial Intelligence and Digital Health Championship, promoting African-led innovation, connected health systems and responsible health data use. A documentary showcased Ethiopia’s investments in digital public infrastructure, electronic health records, community-level digital health systems and artificial intelligence capabilities. Dr Abiy highlighted how technology could improve access to specialist care and overcome geographical and workforce constraints. “A midwife in a remote district should be able to consult a specialist when complications arise. A doctor in a regional hospital should be able to share an image for expert review. And a patient’s medical record should follow them securely from one facility to the next. Distance should no longer mean working alone,” he said. Dr Abiy called for greater investment in African research institutions, laboratories, professional training and locally developed technologies. He also identified three priorities for continental cooperation: establishing centres of medical excellence, strengthening collective purchasing of African-produced medicines and health products, and improving accountability for implementation. Sierra Leone reports progress on maternal and child health President Bio presented results from Sierra Leone’s national campaign to reduce preventable maternal and child deaths and reach children who have missed routine vaccination. Under the campaign, the Ministry of Health, hospitals and district teams conduct weekly reviews of maternal and child deaths to identify contributing factors, assign corrective actions and monitor progress. President Bio reported that maternal deaths had declined by about 34% and child deaths by 12% compared with the corresponding period of the previous year. The campaign had also reached 10,764 previously unvaccinated children, exceeding its target. However, progress remains uneven, particularly in Freetown, where maternal deaths have increased and delays in referral and emergency care persist. The President stressed the need to strengthen emergency obstetric care, improve ambulance referrals and ensure that health facilities have trained personnel, blood supplies and essential medicines. He reaffirmed Sierra Leone’s commitment to increasing domestic health financing through its national health compact and offered to share the country’s emergency response expertise, drawing on lessons from the 2014 Ebola outbreak. Dr Bio also invited African leaders and health teams to learn from Sierra Leone’s weekly accountability reviews. African Union urges greater domestic investment H.E Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, African Union Commission Chairperson called for renewed efforts to meet the Abuja Declaration target of allocating at least 15% of national budgets to health, alongside greater efficiency and accountability in public spending. He emphasised the need to accelerate local pharmaceutical and vaccine manufacturing, invest in African research and innovation, and strengthen the African Medicines Agency, while leveraging the African Continental Free Trade Area and pooled procurement to develop continental health industries. Other priorities included strengthening disease surveillance, early-warning systems, emergency preparedness and the health workforce. The Chairperson stressed that these commitments must translate into better access to vaccines, quality maternal healthcare and timely, affordable treatment. Recognising contributions to public health The opening ceremony honoured African political leaders, scientists and global health partners for their contributions to public health. Presidential Awards for Health Transformation were presented to President Ndayishimiye, as well as Presidents João Lourenço of Angola, John Dramani Mahama of Ghana, Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah of Namibia and Dr Bio. Cameroonian scientist Professor Rose Gana Fomban Leke of the University of Yaoundé received the Distinguished Scientist Award for her contributions to malaria research and immunisation. Extraordinary Global Health Leadership Awards went to Dr Sania Nishtar of Gavi, Dr Richard Hatchett of the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI) and Dr Philippe Duneton of Unitaid, recognising their contributions to vaccine access, epidemic preparedness and equitable access to essential health technologies. ### About Africa CDC Africa CDC is the public health agency of the African Union. As an autonomous institution, Africa CDC supports AU Member States in strengthening health systems, improving disease surveillance, and enhancing emergency preparedness and response. For more information, visit: http://www.africacdc.org and follow Africa CDC on LinkedIn, X, Facebook, and YouTube. Media enquiries: Directorate of Communications and Public Information, Africa CDC | Email: communications@africacdc.org

items.article_text_original: Lima, Peru, 20 November 2026 (PAHO) – The Director of the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, concluded his first official visit to Peru, during which he held meetings with government authorities, congressional representatives, and international organizations to advance shared health priorities, strengthen technical cooperation, and address urgent challenges such as dengue and measles. During his visit, which took place from 16 to 19 November, Dr. Barbosa highlighted several key areas of cooperation, including emergency preparedness and response, particularly in relation to the El Niño phenomenon; strengthening Primary Health Care (PHC); improving care for noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) and mental health; the digital transformation of health systems; and access to vaccines, medicines, and health technologies. “PAHO’s strength lies in how we can contribute to improving the health of countries across the Region. Rather than supporting a country in what it already knows how to do, it is about supporting it to innovate,” the Director said. Agreements to strengthen primary health care and prevent noncommunicable diseases One of the main outcomes of the visit was the signing of two documents aimed at strengthening primary health care and advancing the prevention, early detection, and comprehensive care of NCDs. Dr. Barbosa, together with Minister of Health Luis Dyer Fernández, Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) Health Specialist Ian Mac Arthur, and World Bank Senior Specialist Karina Olivas, participated in the signing of the Record of Establishment of the Consultative Roundtable of the Alliance for Primary Health Care in Peru. The PAHO Director and the Minister of Health also signed the Joint Declaration of the “Better Care for NCDs” initiative. “Primary health care is the best platform for advancing the control of noncommunicable diseases and improving mental health. This initiative allows us to translate our commitment to universal health into concrete action, bringing it closer to individuals and communities,” Dr. Barbosa said. “It is about accompanying countries as they integrate training, process improvements, and access to new technologies, such as telehealth, to work more efficiently and guarantee the right to health.” Health technologies and innovation to improve access to health care During his visit, the Director also participated in the 17th Meeting of the Health Technology Assessment Network of the Americas (RedETSA), held in Lima. The network supports countries in developing their capacity to assess and incorporate health technologies—including medicines, medical devices, strategic supplies, and new treatments—based on the available scientific evidence. At the opening of the meeting, Dr. Barbosa highlighted the opportunities offered by artificial intelligence, digital technologies, and advanced therapies to improve health and quality of life. He also underscored the importance of evaluating these innovations to guide investment decisions and ensure more efficient use of resources. “Health technology assessment provides the knowledge needed to guide innovation in treatments and health policies, remove barriers to access, and make spending more efficient,” he said. “Count on PAHO to support you in the important contribution you are making to ensure equitable access to health innovations for the entire population.” Dengue and measles: responding to immediate public health challenges The prevention and control of dengue and measles featured prominently in the Director's discussions with Peruvian authorities. In response to the increase in dengue cases and deaths in the context of the El Niño phenomenon, PAHO recommended strengthening vector surveillance, preparing health services to effectively manage an increase in cases, and promoting communication strategies that engage communities in preventing and controlling the transmitting mosquito. Dr. Barbosa recalled that while dengue vaccination can help prevent severe forms of the disease, it must be part of a comprehensive response that includes surveillance and vector control. Regarding measles, the Director stressed the importance of increasing vaccination coverage, identifying and actively reaching out to children who have not completed their immunization schedules, and strengthening surveillance to interrupt transmission. Cooperation with national authorities Dr. Barbosa discussed these issues with Minister of Health Luis Dyer Fernández, as well as Vice Minister of Public Health María Sofía Cuba, Vice Minister of Health Services and Insurance Carlos Espinoza, and directors from the Ministry of Health. In addition to meeting with Vice Minister of Foreign Affairs Eric Anderson Machado, the Director met with the President of Congress, Miguel Ángel Torres Morales. Together with the Minister of Health and PAHO/WHO Representative in Peru, Dr. Gustavo Mery, they discussed opportunities for technical cooperation offered by PAHO in the area of digital health transformation, among other priorities. During a meeting with representatives of the health committees of the Congress of the Republic, Dr. Barbosa also highlighted the importance of prioritizing investment in health, strengthening vaccination coverage, particularly against measles, and expanding the multisectoral response to anemia and efforts to address mental health across all population groups. “Senators and members of Congress are important allies in ensuring the right to health. A law has great power to ensure that people can effectively access health services. PAHO seeks to support the country in achieving this,” he said. The Director's agenda also included a meeting with the Executive President of the Social Health Insurance system (EsSalud), Dr. Zulema Tomás, and her technical team to explore opportunities to expand cooperation between the two institutions. PAHO reaffirmed its willingness to support EsSalud in procuring quality medicines and medical supplies through the Regional Revolving Funds. The discussions also addressed the potential of digital transformation, telemedicine, and access to strategic medical equipment to strengthen the response capacity of health facilities and improve care for the millions of people covered by the country's social health insurance system. At the conclusion of his first official visit to Peru, the PAHO Director reaffirmed the Organization's commitment to continuing its work with the country, making its technical cooperation available to support national priorities and initiatives that advance more accessible, resilient health systems capable of responding to the needs of the entire population.

items.article_text_original: The Region’s measles resurgence has resulted in Bolivia, Mexico and the United States losing their measles elimination status, underscoring the urgent need to close vaccination gaps and strengthen surveillance and outbreak response. Washington, D.C., 17 November 2026 (PAHO) – The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) today called on countries across the Americas to intensify efforts to stop measles transmission, close vaccination gaps, and put the Region back on track towards elimination, as outbreaks continue to spread in several parts of the Americas. The call follows the 10–13 November meeting of the Measles, Rubella and Congenital Rubella Syndrome Elimination Regional Monitoring and Re-Verification Commission (RVC), which reviewed the latest epidemiological situation across the Region. Following the Commission’s assessment and recommendations, which were accepted by PAHO Director Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, endemic measles transmission was determined to have been re-established in Bolivia, Mexico, and the United States. All three countries have therefore lost their measles elimination status. Under the Commission’s criteria, endemic transmission is considered re-established when the same measles virus genotype and lineage circulate uninterrupted for 12 months or more in a country. “Losing measles elimination status is much more than losing a public health designation. It means the virus has circulated for a prolonged period, putting families and communities at risk of preventable illness, hospitalization and death," said Dr. Barbosa. The Region of the Americas, the first in the world to eliminate measles, regained its elimination status in 2024 after successfully interrupting endemic transmission in Venezuela and Brazil. However, the loss of regional status in November 2025, following sustained transmission in Canada, was a major setback. The subsequent loss of elimination status by Bolivia, Mexico and the United States marks a further deterioration in the regional situation and makes the path towards restoring elimination more challenging. “This is a serious warning for our Region, but it is not an irreversible setback,” added the PAHO Director. “We know how to prevent measles, and we know how to stop its transmission. With sustained commitment to vaccination, strong surveillance and effective outbreak response, the Americas can eliminate measles transmission once again.” Current situation As of 13 November 2026, the Region has reported 58,213 confirmed measles cases and 82 deaths, compared with 12,806 cases during the same period last year. Bolivia, Mexico and the United States have lost their status after the same measles virus lineage circulated uninterrupted for 12 months or more. All three countries are implementing measures to strengthen vaccination, surveillance and outbreak response. Meanwhile, Canada has interrupted the chain of transmission associated with the outbreak that led to its loss of status and is working to regain elimination status. Measles is one of the most contagious diseases in the world: one infected person can transmit the virus to as many as 18 susceptible individuals. It can cause serious complications, including pneumonia, encephalitis and blindness, and can lead to death. Infection can also weaken the immune system for months afterwards. The resurgence of measles across the Region reflects persistent gaps in population immunity, often concentrated in particular communities and geographic areas. National vaccination figures can mask these disparities, while barriers to health services, missed vaccinations, misinformation and vaccine hesitancy leave children, adolescents and adults vulnerable to infection. Measles is resurging globally amid persistent gaps in vaccination coverage, and several other countries in the Americas are also experiencing prolonged outbreaks. “This situation requires urgent action,” said the PAHO Director. “Continued transmission anywhere increases the risk of the virus reaching people who cannot be vaccinated and communities where immunity gaps persist.” Protecting those who cannot be vaccinated for medical reasons, as well as babies who are too young to receive the vaccine, depends on ensuring that the people around them are protected. PAHO’s response and RVC recommendations PAHO is working with countries to interrupt measles transmission through vaccination campaigns, stronger epidemiological and laboratory surveillance, rapid-response teams and support for outbreak investigation and containment. The RVC has recommended that countries prioritize the following actions to strengthen their efforts to interrupt transmission: - Assess risks and close immunity gaps: Use PAHO’s risk assessment tool to identify high-risk municipalities and populations, prioritizing the most vulnerable. - Strengthen active case finding: Conduct active searches in health facilities, communities and laboratories every three months, and systematically document the results. - Improve classification of suspected vaccine reactions: Apply PAHO criteria, including the timing of rash onset following vaccination, and genotype PCR-positive cases to identify vaccine strains. - Adapt responses to the epidemiological situation: Use PAHO’s July 2026 Measles Preparedness and Response Matrix to guide vaccination, surveillance and laboratory activities, documenting any changes. - Protect health workers: Verify vaccination status, enforce institutional immunization policies and implement airborne isolation protocols. - Ensure timely resources: Equip field teams, remove operational barriers and coordinate government support to enable rapid outbreak response. Sustaining at least 95% coverage with both doses of the measles vaccine in every community remains essential to closing immunity gaps and preventing further transmission. National averages can mask pockets of low coverage, making it critical to reach every community, particularly those most vulnerable to outbreaks. The path back to elimination The Americas has faced this challenge before. After endemic transmission was re-established in Venezuela and Brazil in 2018 and 2019, respectively, countries worked together to interrupt transmission, and the Region regained its measles elimination status in 2024. ”Elimination is not a trophy that we win once and put on a shelf. It must be protected every day by closing immunity gaps and ensuring that every community is reached,” underscored Dr. Barbosa. Achieving and sustaining at least 95% coverage with both doses of the measles vaccine in every community, backed by strong surveillance and effective outbreak response, remains the path towards measles elimination. “PAHO will continue working with every country toward that goal. We know what works. We have done it before. And with sustained commitment and action, the Americas can eliminate measles transmission once again.”

items.article_text_original: As external health financing declines and public health threats persist, Africa’s flagship public health conference will examine progress, confront remaining gaps and advance African-led solutions. Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, 10 November 2026: Africa is entering a defining period for its health security. As external financing becomes increasingly uncertain and public health emergencies continue to test health systems, African countries are strengthening the institutions, capabilities and partnerships needed to take greater ownership of their health future. From continental regulatory cooperation and pooled procurement to local manufacturing, genomic surveillance and emergency response, African-led initiatives are reshaping how the continent prepares for and responds to health challenges. Against this backdrop, the Fifth International Conference on Public Health in Africa (CPHIA 2026) will convene in Addis Ababa from 23 to 27 November, co-hosted by the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) and the Government of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia. Under the theme “Africa’s Health Security and Sovereignty: Transformation from Health Dependency and Vulnerability to Ownership and Resilience,” the conference will bring together African political leaders, policymakers, scientists, health professionals, innovators and partners to examine progress against continental health priorities, identify remaining gaps and advance practical solutions. With more than 30,000 participants expected, CPHIA 2026 will provide an opportunity to assess how continental commitments are translating into stronger institutions, sustainable financing, locally produced health products and better health services for communities. EVENT INFORMATION WHAT: Fifth International Conference on Public Health in Africa (CPHIA 2026) WHEN: 23-27 November 2026 WHERE: Addis International Convention Center, Addis Ababa, Ethiopia CO-HOSTS: Africa CDC and the Government of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia THEME: Africa’s Health Security and Sovereignty: Transformation from Health Dependency and Vulnerability to Ownership and Resilience WHAT TO EXPECT AT CPHIA 2026 CPHIA 2026 will feature high-level political dialogues, scientific discussions, continental initiatives and exchanges on African-led solutions. Discussions will focus on sustainable health financing, local manufacturing, global health architecture reform, digital transformation, artificial intelligence, pandemic preparedness and climate resilience, with particular attention to strengthening Africa’s leadership and ownership of its health systems. Among the major programme highlights are: 22 November – Youth and Women at the Centre of Africa’s Health Future Ahead of the official opening of CPHIA 2026, Africa CDC will convene the Youth Pre-Conference & Women in Health Leadership Summit at Nelson Mandela Hall, African Union Commission, Addis Ababa. The Summit aims to bring together 4,000 young people and 200 women leaders, alongside policymakers, health professionals and innovators, to advance leadership, mentorship, employment opportunities and African-led health solutions. Key anticipated outcomes include a Joint Leadership Declaration and institutional commitments to inform the wider CPHIA 2026 discussions. 23 November – High-Level Opening and Political Leadership The opening day will feature the official ceremony, the high-level launch of the AU Champions’ Roadmap on Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health (RMNCAH) 2026-2030, and two Heads of State panels on leadership and financing for Africa’s health sovereignty. A ministerial dialogue with candidates for the position of Director-General of the World Health Organization (WHO) is scheduled for the afternoon, providing an opportunity for African health leaders to engage on the future of global health leadership. 24 November – Global Health Architecture, Immunisation and Health Financing Discussions will focus on reforming the global health architecture, strengthening continental pandemic preparedness and advancing Africa’s manufacturing ambitions, including the target of producing 60% of its vaccine needs locally by 2040. The programme also features the Continental Immunization Forum launch, the inaugural Continental AIDS Monitoring Report and discussions on the CPHIA Health Financing Pathway Compact. 25 November – Domestic Financing, Local Manufacturing and African Cities High-level sessions will examine sustainable health financing, local manufacturing, regulation and pooled procurement. The programme will also feature the African Cities/Mayors’ Forum and discussions on primary health care, immunisation, malaria vaccines and community engagement. 26 November – Digital Health, Artificial Intelligence and Climate Resilience Plenary sessions will explore digital health, artificial intelligence, data sovereignty and the implications of climate change for Africa’s health security. Additional discussions will address early warning systems, outbreak preparedness and community-centred public health institutions. 27 November – Research, Innovation and the Way Forward The final day will feature discussions on African-led research and development, global health security and the future of primary health care, followed by the official closing ceremony. MEDIA COVERAGE AND INTERVIEW OPPORTUNITIES Accredited media representatives will have opportunities, subject to access and programme arrangements, to cover: • The official opening ceremony and selected high-level sessions. • Scientific discussions and special sessions. • Exhibitions showcasing African innovations and health technologies. • Selected announcements, reports, and partnership initiatives. • Interviews with Africa CDC experts, participating leaders, researchers, innovators and partners, subject to availability. MEDIA ACCREDITATION AND ACCESS Media houses intending to cover CPHIA 2026 are kindly requested to confirm their participation and submit the details of their assigned journalists, photographers and camera crews on or before 20 November 2026 through the link below: Media Registration Form: https://forms.cloud.microsoft/Pages/ResponsePage.aspx?id=RcblrMc-jkyxLgdyIVBd9Wa9aORvrAVHtmNH4wq5MztUMUpUNko2VERSWVVPVjdXRElIUzNWQUNYWi4u&origin=Invitation&channel=0 The information submitted will enable Africa CDC to issue official invitations and facilitate registration fee waivers for eligible media representatives. Journalists who have already registered and received CPHIA 2026 accreditation are encouraged to collect their conference badges in advance and bring them, together with valid identification, to the venue. Further information on media access, designated filming areas, interview requests, and press facilities will be communicated to accredited journalists. Media confirmation and enquiries: Africa CDC Directorate of Communication and Public Information Email: communications@africacdc.org MEDIA RESOURCES Official conference website: https://cphia.africacdc.org/ Conference programme: https://cphia.africacdc.org/programme Africa CDC website: https://africacdc.org/ Official hashtag: #CPHIA2026 END
